clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder of histidine catabolism caused by deficiency of histidase (histidine ammonia-lyase), encoded by HAL.
One of the more common amino acid disorders detected on newborn screening, yet now firmly regarded as a benign condition in the great majority of individuals.

Biochemical hallmark is raised histidine in blood and urine, with increased excretion of imidazolepyruvic acid and related imidazole metabolites; the block prevents conversion of histidine to urocanic acid.
A useful confirmatory finding is absent or markedly reduced urocanic acid in sweat and skin (stratum corneum), reflecting deficient histidase activity in skin as well as liver.
Earlier associations with speech delay and intellectual disability are now attributed to ascertainment bias; large screening cohorts show normal development in nearly all affected children.
A false-positive imidazolepyruvic acid reaction with ferric chloride in urine can mimic phenylketonuria, so histidinaemia must be distinguished from PKU.
Maternal histidinaemia has generally proven benign for the fetus, in contrast to maternal PKU, so routine dietary treatment in pregnancy is not indicated.
No dietary histidine restriction or specific therapy is recommended; management centres on reassurance once the diagnosis is confirmed.
reference.pathophysiology: Histidinaemia is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in HAL, which encodes histidase (histidine ammonia-lyase), the enzyme catalysing the first and committed step of histidine degradation, the non-oxidative deamination of L-histidine to urocanic acid and ammonia. The enzyme is expressed principally in liver and in the stratum corneum of skin. When histidase activity is deficient, histidine accumulates in blood, cerebrospinal fluid and urine, and is instead shunted through transamination to imidazolepyruvic acid and further to imidazoleacetic and imidazolelactic acids, which appear in the urine. The deficiency of skin histidase also causes a characteristic absence of urocanic acid from sweat, a feature exploited diagnostically. Because the downstream products of normal histidine catabolism (ultimately feeding into glutamate and the folate-linked one-carbon pool via formiminoglutamate) are simply reduced rather than replaced by neurotoxic compounds, the accumulation appears metabolically inert, explaining why the condition is clinically benign in the overwhelming majority.
additionalDifferentials: Phenylketonuria (shares a positive urinary ferric chloride test and is the key condition to exclude)
Urocanic aciduria (urocanase/UROC1 deficiency, the next enzyme block in histidine catabolism)
Formiminotransferase deficiency (FTCD, a later histidine-pathway/folate defect with FIGLU excretion)
Transient neonatal hyperhistidinaemia related to prematurity or feeding
Maternal histidinaemia detected through an affected infant's screening
Other benign incidental aminoacidurias found on newborn screening
Secondary histidine elevation in folate deficiency states
additionalInvestigations: Quantitative plasma amino acids demonstrating isolated elevation of histidine
Urine amino acid and organic acid analysis showing imidazolepyruvic, imidazoleacetic and imidazolelactic acids
Measurement of urocanic acid in sweat or skin, characteristically low or absent
Histidase enzyme activity assay in skin (stratum corneum) or liver where indicated
Blood phenylalanine to exclude phenylketonuria after a positive ferric chloride screening reaction
HAL gene analysis to confirm the diagnosis
Follow-up developmental assessment to reassure families rather than to treat
redFlags: A positive urinary ferric chloride test must not be assumed to be histidinaemia until phenylketonuria is excluded
Significant developmental delay or neurological signs should prompt evaluation for an independent cause
Elevated formiminoglutamate (FIGLU) suggests a folate-related or later histidine-pathway defect rather than simple histidinaemia
Any suggestion of a more distal enzyme block (e.g. urocanic aciduria) warrants further metabolic testing
reference.prognosis: Histidinaemia is a benign inborn error of metabolism in nearly all affected individuals, with normal growth, development and life expectancy. Its principal importance is the avoidance of misdiagnosis as phenylketonuria and of unnecessary dietary restriction or investigation.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing histidinaemia as phenylketonuria because of a shared positive ferric chloride urine reaction
Attributing incidental speech delay or intellectual disability to histidinaemia, contrary to modern cohort evidence
Imposing dietary histidine restriction, which is unnecessary and not recommended
Treating maternal histidinaemia as though it carried the fetal risks of maternal phenylketonuria
Failing to consider distal histidine-pathway or folate-related defects when additional metabolites are present
references: Standard inborn errors of metabolism textbooks
Newborn screening and clinical biochemical genetics guidelines
management: Recognise as a benign inborn error requiring no specific therapy or histidine dietary restriction
Reassure the family and avoid unnecessary treatment or investigation
Confirm the diagnosis and exclude phenylketonuria by checking blood phenylalanine after a positive ferric chloride screen
Investigate any unrelated developmental or speech problems on their own merits rather than attributing them to the biochemical finding
Genetic counselling regarding autosomal recessive inheritance for the family
No routine long-term metabolic follow-up once the diagnosis is secure
